My grandmother's kitchen had a radio that murmured news in a language I only half understood. The windows steamed when she cooked rice. I would draw faces in the condensation, and they would vanish before I could name them. Maybe that is what words are: faces drawn on glass, then gone. We keep drawing anyway.

Outside, the city is doing its ordinary miracle. Buses exhale, pigeons argue, someone's dog barks at a leaf. A woman carries groceries in both arms like a sentence with too many commas. A boy on a scooter imagines he is a jet. The world is not waiting for my thousand words. It is already full of them—texts, receipts, headlines, graffiti, love letters never sent, apologies rehearsed in the shower. Language is not scarce. Attention is. The rarest thing is to stop and notice the shape of a moment before it dissolves.

I read once that the average person has thousands of thoughts a day, most of them repeats. The same worries circling like gulls over a parking lot. What if I am wasting my life? What if I am not? What if the people I love are not okay? What if they are, but I am not? The mind is a committee that never agrees. Still, somewhere beneath the noise, there is a quieter voice. It does not shout. It says: look. It says: breathe. It says: this cup of tea is warm, and you are here.

There is a tree outside my window that I have never named. In spring it is extravagant, reckless with blossoms. In summer it is a green argument against the sun. In autumn it lets go, not dramatically, but one leaf at a time, as if it has learned that grief is a process, not an event. In winter it is a skeleton that still believes in spring. I want to be like that tree. Not always beautiful, but faithful to the season. Not always certain, but willing to begin again.

I wonder about the people who will read these words. Maybe no one. Maybe you. If you are reading, you are lending me your eyes and your time, which are the only real currency. Thank you. I do not know your name, your face, the weather where you are. But for a few minutes, we are sharing a silence made of ink and light. We are strangers holding the same thread.

Sometimes I think the internet is a giant mirror broken into a billion pieces, and each piece reflects a different version of us. We scroll, we like, we rage, we laugh, we compare. We have forgotten how to be bored. But maybe we can reclaim it. Let the mind wander until it finds something it did not know it was looking for.

I remember a summer when I was eleven. I spent most of it in a library because it had air conditioning and no one asked me to be anything. I read books about dragons, detectives, planets, pioneers. I fell in love with the smell of paper and the weight of a story. I did not know then that I would spend my life trying to make sentences that felt like that—like a door opening in a wall you thought was solid. I am still trying.

What else comes? Coffee going cold. A train whistle in the distance. The ache in my shoulders from sitting too long. The hope that tomorrow will be different, even if I have no plan. The memory of a stranger who once helped me when my car broke down and refused money. The small kindness of a cashier who said, "Take your time." The way my mother laughs with her whole body. The fear of losing the people I love. The refusal to think about it. The thinking about it anyway.

If I had to give advice, I would say: be where you are. Not because the present is always pleasant, but because it is the only place you can actually live. The past is a museum. The future is a rumor. The present is a room with a window. Open it. Let some air in. Notice what is here. A chair. A heartbeat. A chance to be kind. A chance to begin again. A chance to put down the thousand words and listen.

But I still have words to spend. So let me spend them on this: You are not a machine. You are not a brand. You are a temporary arrangement of stardust and memory, walking around on a rock that spins through space. That is absurd and magnificent. You will make mistakes. You will hurt people. You will be hurt. You will laugh so hard you cry. You will love in ways that make no sense. And through it all, the cursor will blink. Somewhere, a tree will let go of a leaf, trusting the ground.
